source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents (experience-following): add-all vs small fixed store
finding: Adding every execution to memory was worse than keeping a small frozen memory. Only a strict evaluator made add-only beat the fixed store.
numbers: Table 1 (success or accuracy, final memory size). RegAgent: fixed 67.53/100, add-all 55.48/4100, strict 70.95/2938. AgentDriver: fixed 40.11/180, add-all 32.32/2125, strict 51.00/1178. CIC-IoT: fixed 71.50/50, add-all 59.90/1050, strict 85.40/904. EHRAgent: strict 38.50/1012 (fixed and add-all cells hard to read in the PDF layout). Fixed store sometimes beat coarse-evaluator runs.
quote: noisy or low-quality additions can harm memory utility
limits: Four agents, one paper. Strict evaluator is ground truth. EHRAgent fixed/add-all cells are garbled in the text layer, so they are not cited.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 2: an add-only lesson store can be worse than a tiny fixed one (100 vs 4100 records). Pruning is the baseline to beat, not a luxury.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents (experience-following): frequency rule vs utility rule head to head
finding: With a strict evaluator, deleting by average past utility (history-based) beat deleting by retrieval frequency (periodic) on all four agents.
numbers: Strict evaluator, success and final store size. Periodic vs history-based: RegAgent 67.65 (949) vs 69.80 (2286); EHRAgent 38.59 (302) vs 42.06 (784); AgentDriver 50.94 (467) vs 51.81 (846); CIC-IoT 80.80 (310) vs 89.60 (788). No deletion: 70.95/2938, 38.67/1012, 51.00/1178, 85.40/904. Combined: 66.58 (890), 42.34 (248), 49.97 (323), 85.50 (188). Rule: delete if retrieved at least n times and mean utility over those retrievals is below a threshold.
limits: Row-to-strategy mapping read from a garbled table and checked against the prose and the cross-check file. Coarse-evaluator rows too garbled to cite. The frequency rule is a simplified fixed-window retrieval-count threshold.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 (partly closed): outcome-linked deletion beats frequency-style deletion when outcomes are known. Combined rule cut 66 to 79% of records for 0 to 4 points loss on three agents, and gained 3.7 on EHRAgent.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents (experience-following): history-based deletion beats an error-free memory
finding: In AgentDriver, history-based deletion with the strict evaluator beat even an error-free ground-truth-demonstration memory. Deleted records had higher error than retained ones although all had passed the add filter.
numbers: Appendix B.3 and Figure 6 (error density of deleted vs retained records retrieved more than 5 times). Strict addition stored only records with error at most 1; records with error above 0.5 still propagated error.
limits: Evidence is a plot and prose, no test statistic. Error-free baseline run on two agents only.
agent_relevance: The deletion benefit is partly a quality filter that the add step missed (misaligned experience replay), not only a size saving. Fits protection from depression: keep what keeps helping, drop what is retrieved and fails.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents (experience-following): coarse evaluators and the fine-tuned judge
finding: Noisy judges hurt additions, and deletion with a noisy judge gave unstable results. A judge fine-tuned on only 300 correct-judgement examples (C3) recovered most of the gain.
numbers: Table 1, judges C1/C2/C3 (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned on 300 judge examples). RegAgent success 63.18 / 65.78 / 67.35 vs strict 70.95. AgentDriver 36.92 / 40.01 / 47.37 vs strict 51.00 vs add-all 32.32. CIC-IoT 74.00 / 68.80 / 79.50 vs strict 85.40. History deletion with a GPT-4o-mini judge: clear gain on EHRAgent, worse on AgentDriver; fine-tuned judges gave stable results with smaller stores.
limits: Judge quality is not measured as agreement with truth; it is confounded with judge model type. The 300 examples came from a separate ground-truth training set.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: there is no single threshold. A small labelled calibration set (about 300 outcomes) moved a judge from harmful to useful. A self-judge with no outcome signal at all sits below that point.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How memory management impacts LLM agents (experience-following): task distribution shift and fixed capacity
finding: Under a mid-stream task distribution shift, combined deletion stayed close to the no-shift run. Under a hard capacity cap equal to the starting store (100 or 180 records), utility-based deletion still beat the fixed store.
numbers: Section 5.1, Figure 7 (EHRAgent, AgentDriver); Section 5.2, Figure 17 (capacity 100 and 180). On EHRAgent, history-only deletion underperformed combined deletion after the shift; periodic deletion helped stabilise.
limits: The shift was built by reordering the test set, not a real drift. Numbers are only in figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 7: an online prune rule works at a fixed small capacity. Frequency-style (periodic) deletion has a stabilising role under shift when utility history is stale for the new task mix.

source: Zhang et al. (2026, ICLR) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE): context collapse case
finding: When an LLM rewrote the whole accumulated context each step, the context collapsed. One rewrite at step 60 cut 18,282 tokens to 122 tokens and accuracy fell below the no-memory baseline.
numbers: AppWorld case study: step 60 context 18,282 tokens, accuracy 66.7; next step 122 tokens, accuracy 57.1; no-adaptation baseline 63.7.
quote: it collapsed to just 122 tokens, with accuracy dropping to 57.1
limits: Single case study on one benchmark, shown for Dynamic Cheatsheet style monolithic rewriting.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a merge step done as a full LLM rewrite is dangerous. Prune and merge must be per-item edits with counters, never a whole-store rewrite.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) ACE: incremental update ablation (AppWorld)
finding: Removing incremental delta updates removed most of the gain from ACE.
numbers: Offline adaptation, test-normal, DeepSeek-V3.1. ReAct 63.7 TGC / 42.9 SGC (avg 53.3). ACE without incremental updates 67.3 / 46.4 (avg 56.9, +3.6). ACE with incremental updates 76.2 / 64.3 (avg 70.3, +17.0).
limits: Authors' own method and ablation, one base model, one benchmark, no repeats shown.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: itemised edit-in-place updates with a dedupe pass are worth about 13 points over whole-context rewriting. Merge helps only when done as bounded edits.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) ACE: pruning trigger and dedup threshold (FiNER)
finding: Results were flat across a 10x range of the context size at which pruning fires, and across dedup strictness. Ten reflection rounds did worse than five.
numbers: FiNER, DeepSeek-V3.1, base 70.7. Context cap before prune: 10K 78.6 (+7.9), 50K 78.4 (+7.7), 100K 78.3 (+7.6). Dedup threshold 50% 77.0, 70% 73.9, 90% 78.6. AppWorld reflection rounds, average score: 1 round 61.3, 3 rounds 65.8, 5 rounds 67.6, 10 rounds 65.2 (no-ACE 53.3).
limits: Flat on FiNER only; those contexts may never get large enough to need pruning. No no-pruning arm in the table. The 70% dedup dip is unexplained.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no sharp interior optimum for the prune trigger at this scale. There is a small inverted U on extraction effort (rounds), not on store size.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) ACE: feedback quality limits
finding: ACE worked without ground-truth labels when execution signals existed (AppWorld). With no reliable feedback (finance), ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet could degrade.
numbers: AppWorld no-label: average +14.8% over ReAct. Harmful reflector every X steps on FiNER (base 70.7): X=1 66.7 (-4.0), X=5 76.1 (+5.4), X=10 77.0, X=25 77.8, X=50 and 100 78.2, never 78.3. Weaker Reflector GPT-OSS-120B 76.6 vs DeepSeek-V3.1 78.3.
quote: context adaptation depends critically on feedback quality
limits: Harm was injected on purpose and at random; real self-judge error is correlated with the task. The finance degradation is stated in prose with no number in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the gain survived one corrupted update in five and turned negative only when every update was corrupted. Executable signals (tests, code runs) are a usable utility signal.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: full history vs curated memory
finding: Appending all past input-output pairs (full history, FH) was worse than curated memory, and could be worse than no memory.
numbers: AIME 2024: Claude 3.5 Sonnet FH 26.7% vs DC-based 50.0%. GPT-4o baseline 20.0%, FH 6.7%, DC-RS 40.0%. Majority vote of 3 on AIME 2025 stayed at 6.7%.
quote: Excessive uncurated input-output pairs can not only overwhelm the model's context window
limits: Small benchmarks (30 questions per AIME year), single runs. GPT-4o-mini and Haiku gained little or fell below baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 8: add-everything is not neutral; it cut GPT-4o by 13 points on a real benchmark. Memory benefit depends on the base model producing correct entries.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: model dependence and rewrite failure
finding: Small models gained little or lost under test-time memory. The curator sometimes wrote a stub like 'previous content preserved' instead of rewriting, which shrank memory silently.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini AIME 2024: DC- +20.0 points, DC-Cu and DC-RS below baseline. GPT-4o GPQA-Diamond 57.1 to 58.1 under DC-RS. Claude 3.5 Sonnet GPQA-Diamond 59.6 to 68.7 (retrieval only 63.6). GPT-4o Game of 24 10% to 99% under DC-RS.
limits: Authors give the truncation problem qualitatively; no frequency is counted.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 5: base-model generation quality gates memory benefit; a rewrite-based curator can lose content without anyone noticing.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: vote-and-remove insights and what experience is needed
finding: Each insight has a count: ADD starts it, UPVOTE or EDIT raises it, DOWNVOTE lowers it, and it is removed at zero. Insights alone and retrieval alone each beat ReAct; together they beat each.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. ExpeL matched Reflexion at R3 on HotpotQA (40% vs 39%) and ALFWorld (54% vs 59%). Insights extracted only from the initial few-shot examples gave no gain over ReAct; adding reflections to the insight prompt hurt.
limits: No ablation of the removal rule or of the insight count, so the vote rule is not isolated. Ablation table values are garbled in the text layer; only prose results are used.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the vote-and-remove rule exists but has never been tested alone. Insights need real success/failure experience first: no experience, no gain.

source: Chauhan et al. (2026) RSPM: failure mode of pruning on a hard task
finding: Pruning on failure can hurt. On one LoCoMo conversation with a 35% natural error rate, the sleep cycle fired 21 times, pruned 43% of the store, and ended 19.5 points below baseline.
numbers: Aggregate: LoCoMo-10, 3,850 evaluations, 72.8% accuracy, +7.6 over RAG (p=0.0042); store flattens near 472 entries vs 675 (about 30% fewer). SWE-bench simulation 40.0 to 49.1 (+9.1, p=0.0003, 10 seeds). Temporal consistency 92.5% vs RAG 80.6% vs oracle conflict labels 88.4% vs keyword detector 79.5%. Sleep every 10 tasks and on a failure spike; promotion after 3 then 5 contexts.
quote: a memory involved in a failure caused it
limits: Three-page paper, simulated SWE-bench, the failing conversation reported only in prose. Template header says NeurIPS 2023.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 6: the rule 'a memory used in a failed task caused the failure' breaks when the task is simply hard. Cap the prune fraction per cycle. A keyword conflict detector was worse than no pruning; an LLM detector was better.

source: Chauhan et al. (2026) RSPM: consolidation into rules plus deletion
finding: RSPM merges failure clusters into rules and deletes the raw episodes. The authors say removing the sleep cycle cost the most, but give no table.
numbers: At 19,008 simulated SWE-bench issues: 3,438 repo-specific constraints, 24 error-class rules, 18 universal rules. Gain grows with difficulty, +5.4 points for issues under 15 minutes to +13.2 over four hours. Retry loops 5.9% to 6.7% of attempts.
limits: No ablation numbers in the text and no prune-only arm, so prune-only vs prune-plus-merge is not separated. The 93% fewer retry loops figure is an abstract claim only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: no study separates deletion from distillation in a lesson store at equal tokens. Gap 10: one self-benchmarked paper, not a replication.

source: Wei et al. (2026) FadeMem: component ablation (decay, fusion, conflict)
finding: In FadeMem, removing the fusion (merge) step hurt most, more than removing the dual-layer decay or conflict resolution. Storage fell 45%.
numbers: LoCoMo multi-hop F1: full 29.43; without dual-layer 19.45 (-33.9%); without fusion 13.63 (-53.7%); without conflict resolution 22.88 (-22.4%). Mem0 28.37. LTI-Bench: critical facts retained 82.1% at 55.0% storage vs Mem0 78.4% at 100%, MemGPT 75.6% at 85.3%.
limits: Judge-model scores and a 30-day simulated benchmark; margin over Mem0 about 1 F1. Ablation is a bar chart with numbers in prose. Not independent.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 (weak): merge mattered most when decay was also on. Authors are the same, so treat as a hint, not evidence of a prune-versus-merge effect.

source: Xie (2026) SleepGate: decay-only and attention-based retention in a toy model
finding: A trained forgetting gate beat decay-only by a wide margin. H2O (keep entries with highest cumulative attention) was worst because the most-used entries were the stale ones.
numbers: 793K-parameter transformer, 200 episodes per depth, accuracy / stale rate. SleepGate n=2 99.0/0.5, n=5 99.5/0.0, n=10 97.0/3.5, n=15 73.5/23.5, n=20 30.5/55.5, n=30 16.5/62.0. Decay-only 12.5 at n=2 and 7.5 at n=10. H2O 7.5 at n=2. StreamingLLM 18.0 at n=2. Full KV cache 9.0 at n=2.
quote: retaining heavy hitters actively preserves interference
limits: Synthetic tokens and a 4-layer toy model; the gate was trained with supersession labels. Sharp failure from n=15 because gate signatures cannot separate near-identical entries.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a use-count rule keeps stale favourites, and age-decay alone gave nothing here. Supersession detection (a conflict signal) was what worked. Gap 9: the benefit vanishes past about 15 near-duplicates.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory: offline vs online induction
finding: Inducing workflows offline from training examples and online from the agent's own test-time runs gave similar results in-domain. Online was better when training tasks did not match test tasks.
numbers: Mind2Web (GPT-4) step SR cross-task / cross-website / cross-domain: MindAct 36.2 / 30.1 / 18.6; AWM offline 45.1 / 33.7 / 32.6; AWM online 43.6 / 33.9 / 35.5. Task SR offline 4.8 / 2.3 / 0.7, online 4.0 / 1.6 / 1.7.
limits: AWM adds but does not delete, so this compares where memory is built, not wake vs sleep pruning. Task success is very low; one or two point gaps are noise-level.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: weak, indirect evidence that online, in-task memory formation is not worse than a separate offline pass and is better under distribution shift. No prune pass was compared.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: bounded episodic memory
finding: Reflexion keeps only the last 1 to 3 reflections as a sliding window because of the context limit. The authors say future work could extend memory.
numbers: Memory limit set to 1 to 3 experiences; the AlfWorld run used 3; the reasoning task used a limit of 1.
quote: a sliding window with maximum capacity
limits: A hard first-in-first-out cap, not a pruning policy. No ablation of the cap size in the text read.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the most common deployed 'prune' is a tiny FIFO window (1 to 3 items). It has never been compared with utility-based pruning at the same size.
